Indicator charts in R

Source: vignettes/golemworldbank.Rmd
golemworldbank.Rmd

The charts and tables of the golemworldbank app are also R functions. They take the World Bank data that comes with the package and return an interactive plotly chart or a DT table. Run one in the console and it opens in the RStudio Viewer or your browser. In an R Markdown or Quarto document it appears in the page.

This article shows the data and the line charts of the Country Comparison and Indicator Comparison tabs. Animated charts shows the population pyramid, the bar chart race, the bubble chart and the map, and Changes and the indicator index shows the tables of the Change (%) and Index tabs.

Install and load the package 

install.packages("golemworldbank",
  repos = c("https://sedzinfo.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
library(golemworldbank)

run_app() starts the app itself on your computer:

run_app()

The data

The data comes with the package: the World Development Indicators of World Bank Open Data. mfi_table() gives the values of the indicators, a row per country, indicator and year: 217 countries, 1,497 indicators and the years 1960 to 2025. Missing values are not in it, and neither are regions and income groups such as “World”. For example, the last years of the population of Greece:

greece <- subset(mfi_table(), `Country Name` == "Greece" &
                   `Indicator Name` == "Population, total")
tail(greece)
#>         Country Code Country Name    Indicator Name Year    value
#> 6675414          GRC       Greece Population, total 2020 10698599
#> 6856141          GRC       Greece Population, total 2021 10570130
#> 7028682          GRC       Greece Population, total 2022 10437805
#> 7192041          GRC       Greece Population, total 2023 10407351
#> 7340692          GRC       Greece Population, total 2024 10405134
#> 7454480          GRC       Greece Population, total 2025 10413962

The package stores this table as the dataset mfi, with the names of the countries and indicators as codes, which keeps its file small. mfi_table() turns them back into text the first time it is called and keeps the table in memory for the next calls, so the examples below call it in every chart.

Three more datasets come with the package:

  • mfi_population, the share of each five-year age group in the male and in the female population, per country and year, for the population pyramid;
  • country_code, the World Bank’s metadata of each country, such as its region and income group, which give the bubble chart its colors;
  • indicator_info, the World Bank’s topic and definition of every indicator.

Find countries and indicators

The functions take the names of the countries and indicators as they are in the data. To list them:

countries <- sort(unique(mfi_table()$`Country Name`))
writeLines(head(countries))
#> Afghanistan
#> Albania
#> Algeria
#> American Samoa
#> Andorra
#> Angola
indicators <- unique(mfi_table()$`Indicator Name`)
writeLines(grep("^GDP per capita", indicators, value = TRUE))
#> GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)
#> GDP per capita (constant LCU)
#> GDP per capita (current LCU)
#> GDP per capita (current US$)
#> GDP per capita growth (annual %)
#> GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $)
#> GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)

indicator_info gives the topic and definition of an indicator:

info <- indicator_info[indicator_info$`Indicator Name` == "Population, total", ]
info$Topic
#> [1] "Health: Population: Structure"
writeLines(strwrap(info$Definition, 70))
#> Total population is based on the de facto definition of population,
#> which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship.
#> The values shown are midyear estimates.

Changes and the indicator index shows the definitions in a table that can be searched.

Compare countries

plot_country_comp() draws one indicator over the years, with a line per country, as the Country Comparison tab does. Hover over a point for its country, indicator, year and value:

plot_country_comp(
  mfi_table(),
  countries = c("Greece", "Bulgaria"),
  indicator = "Population, total",
  font_style = font_style
)

A click on a country in the legend hides or shows its line.

Compare indicators

plot_indicator_comp() draws several indicators of one country, with a line per indicator, as the Indicator Comparison tab does. The indicators share one y axis, so they compare well only when they have the same unit and a similar scale, such as the female and the male population:

plot_indicator_comp(
  mfi_table(),
  country = "Greece",
  indicators = c("Population, female", "Population, male"),
  font_style = font_style
)

The font

Every chart takes a font_style: the font of its text, which goes to plotly::layout(font = ). font_style, which comes with the package, is the font of the app: 20 px, bold and dark gray. For another font, pass a list of your own, such as a smaller size:

plot_country_comp(
  mfi_table(),
  countries = c("Greece", "Bulgaria", "Romania"),
  indicator = "GDP per capita (current US$)",
  font_style = list(size = 12)
)

Save or change a chart

The charts are plotly objects, so the functions of the plotly and htmlwidgets packages work on them. To save a chart as a web page that opens in any browser:

chart <- plot_country_comp(
  mfi_table(),
  countries = c("Greece", "Bulgaria"),
  indicator = "Population, total",
  font_style = font_style
)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(chart, "population.html")

To change the layout, for example the title:

plotly::layout(chart, title = "Population of Greece and Bulgaria")

The package exports the pipe %>%, so the changes can also be chained:

chart %>%
  plotly::layout(title = "Population of Greece and Bulgaria") %>%
  htmlwidgets::saveWidget("population.html")
